reason: The sources provide over a dozen corroborated facts across independent domains detailing V404 Cygni's recurring outbursts and wobbling relativistic jets.
story: About 8,000 light-years away in the constellation Cygnus lies V404 Cygni, a stellar-mass black hole roughly nine to ten times the mass of the Sun. Locked in a tight 6.5-day orbit with a companion star, the black hole steadily siphons off gas into an accretion disk. For decades, this matter accumulates quietly like water behind a dam. But every twenty to thirty years—recorded in 1938, 1956, 1989, and 2015—the system reaches a breaking point. When it woke in June 2015 after 26 years of dormancy, a tsunami of superheated plasma rushed inward, unleashing blinding bursts of radiation that made it the brightest X-ray source in the sky, up to 50 times brighter than the Crab Nebula. Even more terrifyingly, intense gravitational frame-dragging caused the inner disk to wobble like a dying top, whipping relativistic plasma jets across space in rapidly shifting directions within minutes.
angle: When this sleeping black hole wakes up, extreme space-time warping causes its relativistic plasma jets to wobble like a spinning top, spraying high-energy bullets in wildly changing directions within minutes.

claims.claim: V404 Cygni is located in the constellation Cygnus.
The system is situated approximately 7,800 to 8,000 light-years away from Earth.
The system contains a stellar-mass black hole.
The black hole has a mass estimated between 9 and 10 solar masses.
A companion star orbits the black hole in a tight binary orbit of approximately 6.5 days.
Intense gravity pulls matter from the companion star into an accretion disk surrounding the black hole.
V404 Cygni underwent recorded outbursts in 1938 and 1956 prior to the space age.
On May 22, 1989, an outburst from the system was discovered by Japan's Ginga satellite team and cataloged as GS 2023+338.
Instruments aboard Russia's Mir space station observed the 1989 outburst.
Following its 1989 outburst, the black hole slumbered for 26 years until waking up on June 15, 2015.
NASA's Swift satellite detected the initial flare-up of the June 2015 outburst.
The European Space Agency's INTEGRAL gamma-ray observatory carried out extensive monitoring of the 2015 outburst.
During peak flashes in 2015, V404 Cygni became the brightest object in the X-ray sky, reaching up to 50 times the brightness of the Crab Nebula.
Relativistic jets shot from the black hole change orientation and wobble on timescales of minutes to hours.
The jet precession is driven by Lense-Thirring frame dragging due to misalignment between the black hole's spin axis and the accretion disk.
In 2024, astronomers confirmed that V404 Cygni is a hierarchical triple star system with an outer tertiary star orbiting at least 3,500 AU away over roughly 70,000 years.

disputed: Black hole mass estimate: S1 and S6 state about 9 solar masses, whereas S2 states 10 times the Sun's mass; a script should attribute this as roughly 9 to 10 solar masses.

Evolutionary classification of the companion star: S1 classifies it as an early K giant, while S6 classifies it as a subgiant; a script should describe it generally as an evolved star slightly less massive than the Sun.

Cause of spin-orbit misalignment: S3 suggests the tilt may result from a supernova natal kick, whereas S1 and S6 cite recent 2024 findings indicating a minimal natal kick under 5 km/s; a script should avoid asserting a specific cause for the tilt.
